Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › Learning Objectives
Method selection

Choose bottom-up when connectivity is absent. Choose top-down when some services work and others do not. Choose divide-and-conquer to isolate a segment or device affecting only part of the network.

Mnemonic
Think: 'Start where failure makes the most sense' — physical for total outages, application for service-specific problems.
Safe testing and tools
  • Use ping and tracert to check reachability and path.
  • Use Test-NetConnection or telnet to validate specific ports like TCP 445 for SMB.
  • Make one change at a time and document it.
Verified competency milestone
Example commands
ping fileserver_ip_address
tracert fileserver_ip_address
Test-NetConnection -ComputerName fileserver -Port 445
Run these commands to confirm reachability, routing, and port accessibility before changing configurations.

screens.title: Why a Systematic Troubleshooting Approach?
screens.narratorSegment: A systematic troubleshooting approach is the difference between repeating the same outage and resolving it efficiently. At its core, systematic troubleshooting means using a consistent sequence of steps to collect facts, form hypotheses, test them, and document outcomes. This prevents 'shotgun troubleshooting' where multiple changes are made at once and nobody knows which change solved the problem. Think of troubleshooting as a scientific method applied to networks: gather observations, propose an explanation, design a test that will confirm or reject the explanation, run the test, and record the result. For example, if a user reports no connectivity and there are no link lights, the likely root cause is physical. If you instead applied high-level fixes, you might waste time reconfiguring services that depend on basic link status. A common misconception is that experience alone replaces process; in reality, without a repeatable method even experienced technicians can overlook simple checks. The practical benefit is measurable: less time spent, fewer repeated outages, and a growing documentation set that accelerates future work. Before you change any configuration, ask: what is my hypothesis and how will this test it?

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › Systematic Troubleshooting
Definition
A repeatable, hypothesis-driven process

Apply consistent steps to reduce time spent chasing symptoms and increase chance of finding the root cause.

Common misconception

Experience alone is not a substitute for process; even seasoned technicians should follow a method to avoid missing simple checks.

Key Takeaway

Always form a clear hypothesis and design a test that will confirm or reject it before making changes.

Process cards — think like an investigator
Gather facts
Logs, error messages, user description, recent changes.
Form hypothesis
A concise, testable explanation of the observed symptom.
Test & verify
Run a controlled test, observe results, and roll forward or back accordingly.
Concrete example
No link lights: hypothesis — physical layer fault. Test — re-seat cable and check link light. If that fixes it, document the fix and any preventative steps.

screens.title: Using the OSI Model as a Diagnostic Framework
screens.narratorSegment: The OSI model divides network functionality into seven conceptual layers, and that division is an effective diagnostic checklist. When you map observed symptoms to layers, you prioritize checks and avoid irrelevant changes. For instance, a cable failure is a physical layer problem; an incorrect IP address is a network layer issue; and a misconfigured file service is an application layer concern. Using the OSI model means you can rule out whole categories quickly. Start with a claim: where does the symptom best fit — link failure, unreachable IP, or failed login? Then perform the checks associated with that layer. A key benefit is that you can escalate or hand off with precise information: rather than saying 'network is broken,' you can say 'Layer 3 routing to the server is failing,' which focuses subsequent work. A common misconception is to treat the OSI model as rigid order; instead, use it as a guide. Depending on context, you might start at the top or bottom. The important part is isolating the layer so you can apply the right tools and commands. Using the OSI Model as a Diagnostic Framework means map symptoms to layers to focus checks and communicate precise findings to teammates.. In practical terms, a seven-layer checklist for isolating problems. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › OSI Model
Layer hierarchy
7
Application — service behavior, authentication, application errors
6
Presentation — encoding or format issues
5
Session — connections and sessions management
4
Transport — ports, reliability, TCP/UDP
3
Network — IP addressing and routing
2
Data Link — MAC addresses, switches, VLANs
1

Communication tip

Report the suspected layer when escalating: it sharpens the next responder's focus and saves time.

Example mappings
Physical
No link lights, loose cable, failed NIC.
Network
Incorrect IP, wrong gateway, routing table errors.
Transport
Port blocked or service not listening.
Application
Authentication failures, misconfigured share paths.
Key Takeaway

Use the OSI layers as a focused checklist, not a rigid sequence; choose the start point that fits the symptom.

screens.title: Physical and Data Link Checks (Layers 1–2)
screens.narratorSegment: Layers 1 and 2 are where the network meets physical reality. When a device cannot access any network resources, start here. A basic sequence: visually inspect cable connections, confirm link lights on NIC and switch, check switch port status and VLAN membership, and confirm MAC address presence in the switch table if you have access. These checks are fast and often resolve simple faults caused by loose cables, port moves, or incorrect VLAN assignments. For example, a user whose machine has no link lights likely has a physical issue; re-seating the cable and testing the port typically resolves it. A common misconception is that modern networks 'just work' so we can skip these checks — skipping them wastes time if the root cause is physical. If physical checks pass, move up the layers. Remember to follow safety and access policies before touching equipment. Keep a quick checklist: cable, link lights, port status, VLAN, MAC table. This short routine removes a large portion of transient incidents and gives you confidence to proceed when nothing obvious appears. Physical and Data Link Checks (Layers 1–2) means fast physical and switch-level checks remove many simple causes before deeper investigation.. In practical terms, basic connectivity checks you should always perform first. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › Layers 1–2
Checklist
  1. Visually inspect cables and connectors for damage or looseness.
  2. Confirm link lights on NIC and switch port.
  3. Check switch port status and VLAN membership.
  4. Verify MAC address appears in switch MAC table if accessible.
Concrete example

User with no connectivity had a laptop dock partially seated. Re-seating the dock restored link lights and network access.

Common mistake

Skipping physical checks and jumping to complex configuration changes wastes time and risks creating new issues.

Quick tool examples
Link light check is visual. If you have switch access, run a port status command to confirm admin state and link state.
Switch verification
# Example switch commands vary by vendor
show interfaces status
show mac address-table interface Gi1/0/5
These checks confirm port status and whether the device MAC is learned on the expected port.

screens.title: Network and Transport Layer Checks (Layers 3–4)
screens.narratorSegment: Once physical and data link checks are clear, move to Layers 3 and 4. Layer 3 checks address IP addressing and routing: confirm the device has a valid IP, correct subnet mask, and appropriate default gateway. Use ping to verify reachability and tracert to inspect the path a packet takes to a destination. If routing is incorrect, tracert often shows where packets stop being forwarded. At Layer 4, verify transport-level connectivity: ensure the service port is open and the target service is listening. Commands like Test-NetConnection or telnet to a port help determine whether a TCP handshake succeeds. For SMB shares, for example, verify TCP 445. A common misconception is to assume reachability equals service availability; a host can respond to ping but still have its application port blocked by a firewall or not listening. Your hypothesis should reflect the symptom: unreachable IP suggests Layer 3; reachable IP but closed port suggests Layer 4. Always document the commands you ran and their outputs so the next person understands what was tested and why. Network and Transport Layer Checks (Layers 3–4) means use ping and tracert for routing issues; use port checks to confirm services at the transport layer.. In practical terms, ip reachability, routing, and port verification. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › Layers 3–4
Layer 3 checks
  • Confirm IP, subnet mask, and default gateway.
  • Use ping to verify reachability.
  • Use tracert to reveal routing path and failures.
Layer 4 checks
  • Verify the service port is open and listening.
  • Use Test-NetConnection or telnet to test a TCP port.
  • Check firewalls or ACLs blocking the port.
Command examples
ping fileserver_ip_address
tracert fileserver_ip_address
Test-NetConnection -ComputerName fileserver -Port 445
# or
telnet fileserver 445
Key Takeaway

Reachability and service availability are distinct; verify both IP path and transport ports when diagnosing access issues.

screens.title: Session, Presentation, and Application Checks (Layers 5–7)
screens.narratorSegment: Layers 5 through 7 handle sessions, data representation, and the actual application services the user interacts with. When a user can reach an IP and a port but cannot access a service, start looking here. For example, a shared drive that fails to open despite successful port checks could indicate incorrect share paths, permissions, or authentication failures. Verify the user's credentials, check server logs for authentication errors, and confirm the service is configured to accept connections from that client. Presentation issues, like encoding or protocol mismatches, are less common in basic file sharing but can appear in application stacks that require specific negotiation. A helpful approach is to reproduce the failure from another client or from the server itself to distinguish client vs server problems. A frequent misconception is treating application errors as network issues; testing whether the application works locally on the server helps identify where the error originates. Always include these high-level checks before making assumptions about routing or physical causes when service-specific symptoms appear. Session, Presentation, and Application Checks (Layers 5–7) means if reachability and ports are confirmed, investigate sessions, authentication, and application configuration for the root cause.. In practical terms, authentication, sessions, and application configuration issues. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › Layers 5–7
What to check
  • Authentication: verify user credentials and check server logs for failures.
  • Session state: confirm sessions are established and not timing out.
  • Application config: ensure service paths, permissions, and bindings are correct.
Concrete example

User can ping the file server and port 445 responds, but access is denied because the user account lacks share permissions. Fixing permissions resolves the issue without touching network settings.

Misconception

Assuming every access failure is a network problem. Validate application behavior locally on the server to separate app errors from network faults.

Reproduction strategy
  1. Attempt access from another client on the same network segment.
  2. Attempt access locally on the server (loopback or local tools).
  3. Compare logs and error messages to identify authentication vs network causes.

screens.title: Bottom-Up, Top-Down, and Divide-and-Conquer
screens.narratorSegment: There are three widely used troubleshooting methodologies and each fits different scenarios. Bottom-up starts at the physical layer and moves upward; it is effective when there is no connectivity at all. Top-down starts at the application layer and moves downward; it is useful when some services are working but a specific application fails. Divide-and-conquer isolates the failing segment or device by comparing affected and unaffected groups, which is powerful when only part of the network is impacted. To choose: when a user has zero network access, bottom-up quickly rules out cabling and ports. When a specific service fails while others work, top-down narrows down service or session issues. If only one department is affected, divide-and-conquer limits focus to that segment. A common error is applying the wrong method and wasting time. For example, running switch port checks (bottom-up) when only one application fails is inefficient. Instead, start where the symptom logically belongs. Each method still benefits from forming a hypothesis and testing it; methodologies guide your starting point and order of checks, not replace disciplined testing and documentation. Bottom-Up, Top-Down, and Divide-and-Conquer means match your starting approach—bottom-up, top-down, or divide-and-conquer—to the observed symptoms for efficient diagnosis.. In practical terms, choose the right methodology based on symptoms. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › Methodologies
Bottom-Up
Start at Layer 1 and work up. Best when there is no connectivity at all. Quick wins: cables, link lights, port state.
Top-Down
Start at Layer 7 and work down. Best when a particular service or application fails while others succeed. Focus on sessions, permissions, and app config.
Divide-and-Conquer
Isolate the fault by comparing affected and unaffected users or segments. Best for partial outages limited to a group or topology section.
Decision guidance
Ask: does the symptom affect everything, a service, or a segment? Use that answer to pick the methodology, then form a hypothesis and test.

screens.title: Structured Troubleshooting Steps
screens.narratorSegment: A structured troubleshooting process is a sequence of repeatable steps that keeps your investigation clear and auditable. Begin by defining the problem precisely: collect exact symptoms, error messages, and the time the issue began. Next, gather information using monitoring tools, device logs, and simple commands. Use that data to formulate one or more hypotheses — concise, testable explanations for the observed behavior. Prioritize hypotheses by likelihood and impact. Test the highest-priority hypothesis with minimal, reversible changes or non-invasive diagnostics. If the test confirms your hypothesis, implement a permanent fix and verify full functionality. If not, revert any temporary changes and move to the next hypothesis. Finally, document what you observed, the tests you ran, the successful fix, and any preventative measures. A common mistake is skipping documentation or making multiple simultaneous changes; that makes rollback and learning difficult. This process turns incidents into learning opportunities and builds a knowledge base that accelerates future resolutions. Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › Troubleshooting Steps
Step list
  1. Define the problem with precise symptoms.
  2. Gather information: logs, configs, command outputs.
  3. Formulate a hypothesis.
  4. Test the hypothesis with controlled checks.
  5. Implement the permanent solution if confirmed.
  6. Verify full functionality and absence of side effects.
  7. Document the incident and preventative steps.
Pro tip

Make changes that are reversible and test immediately to know whether the change helped.

Scenario mapping
When a shared drive fails, follow the steps: define the exact path and error, gather network and server logs, hypothesize which layer is likely at fault, test using ping and port checks, implement fixes like permission updates or route corrections, verify by reproducing the access, and document the fix and recommended prevention.
Key Takeaway

A repeatable step sequence reduces mistakes and creates shareable documentation for teams.

screens.title: Testing Hypotheses and One-Change Discipline
screens.narratorSegment: Testing a hypothesis is the central act of troubleshooting. A good hypothesis is specific and falsifiable: it states a likely cause and predicts what will happen when you test it. For example, hypothesizing 'the user has the wrong default gateway' predicts that correcting the gateway will restore connectivity. Design a test that is minimally invasive and reversible. Make only one change at a time, then test. This one-change discipline prevents confusion about which action fixed the issue and makes rollback straightforward if the change causes unintended effects. A frequent real-world mistake is 'shotgun troubleshooting' — changing multiple settings hoping one will work — which destroys the audit trail and can create new problems. Always capture the state before the change, what you changed, and the test results. That documentation is vital for post-incident review and for team learning. Over time, your documented tests and results form a knowledge base that accelerates future troubleshooting. Testing Hypotheses and One-Change Discipline means design reversible tests, change one variable at a time, and record outcomes to know what actually fixed the issue.. In practical terms, make one change, test, and document the result. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

One-change discipline

Documentation example

screens.title: Documentation, Safety, and Handoffs
screens.narratorSegment: Documentation is often the most undervalued skill in troubleshooting. Recording symptoms, commands, test results, and the final resolution creates a knowledge base that shortens future troubleshooting and enables safe handoffs between technicians. Good documentation includes timestamps, the exact commands run, the change that fixed the issue, and any follow-up recommendations. Safety matters when you need physical access: verify authorization, de-energize equipment if required, and follow organizational safety protocols to avoid physical harm or accidental outages. When handing off, report the layer you isolated, the hypothesis you tested, the commands and results, and the permanent solution applied. A common mistake is assuming the next person will infer what happened — never assume. Clear documentation reduces repeat incidents, accelerates training, and preserves institutional memory. Treat every incident as an opportunity to add one practical prevention step to reduce recurrence. screens.title: Applying the OSI Model: Shared Drive Scenario
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk a real scenario: a user cannot access \\fileserver\shared but can browse the internet. Step one, define the problem precisely: confirm the exact path, the error message, and whether other users have the same issue. Step two, gather information: ping the file server IP, run tracert, and test TCP 445 with Test-NetConnection or telnet. If ping succeeds and port 445 is reachable, move to higher-layer checks: verify credentials and server share permissions and look for authentication failures in logs. If the port is closed or tracert fails, the fault is likely Layer 3 or 4 and you should investigate routing and firewall rules. Use divide-and-conquer if only one department is affected — test from a different segment. Form a hypothesis, for example, 'SMB port blocked by a firewall rule between the user and server,' and design a test like temporarily allowing the port for the client segment. Make one change at a time. After confirmation, implement the permanent fix and document the exact commands, the successful test results, and preventative recommendations. Reflection: given that internet browsing works but the share does not, which OSI layer is the best starting point and why?

fullNarratorScript:
Troubleshooting networks is a process, not a guessing game. In this lesson you will learn why a systematic methodology reduces downtime, how the OSI model gives you a logical way to isolate faults, and which common approaches help you pinpoint problems quickly. You will see concrete tactics like starting at the physical layer to confirm basic connectivity, forming and testing hypotheses, and recording every change so future incidents resolve faster. For example, when a user can browse the internet but cannot open a shared drive, the OSI model helps you ask the right questions: is it an access control issue, a blocked port, a routing problem, or a local cable? We will compare bottom-up, top-down, and divide-and-conquer strategies and practice a step-by-step process that includes defining the problem, gathering information, hypothesizing causes, testing, verifying, and documenting. You will also learn common mistakes to avoid, such as making multiple simultaneous changes or stopping before full verification. By the end of this chapter you will have a practical, repeatable workflow to isolate and resolve network issues, and a short checklist to use on the job. Which step will you try first the next time connectivity breaks?

Over the next slides you will gain four practical competencies that make you an effective first-line network troubleshooter. First, you will explain why a systematic troubleshooting approach matters and how it saves time by isolating root causes. Second, you will use the OSI model as a diagnostic framework so you can narrow a problem to a specific layer rather than guessing. Third, you will perform a structured troubleshooting process: define the problem, gather information, form a hypothesis, test, implement, verify, and document. Fourth, you will recognize common mistakes, such as making multiple changes at once or failing to verify, and learn how to avoid them. Each objective includes an example or mnemonic to help you remember. For instance, the define-gather-hypothesize-test pattern is a reliable sequence to follow on every incident. By practicing these objectives with a scenario, you will build muscle memory and a checklist to use in the field. These skills are valuable because they reduce downtime, improve confidence, and create repeatable outcomes for teams that support production networks.

This second objectives screen emphasizes practical application and safe behavior around live equipment. You will learn how to choose a troubleshooting methodology based on symptoms: bottom-up when there is no connectivity, top-down when services partially work, and divide-and-conquer when problems are isolated to a segment or device. You will practice forming a clear hypothesis so your tests are purposeful rather than random. Testing should include reproducible commands and checks, such as ping for reachability, tracert for path issues, and Test-NetConnection or telnet to verify TCP ports. You will also learn the discipline of 'one change, one test' and the importance of documenting each step so that teams can reproduce or roll back changes. Finally, safety and authorization are part of competency: obtain permission before touching live infrastructure and follow electrical and organizational safety rules. Together, these objectives prepare you to resolve incidents confidently while protecting production services and improving future response.

A systematic troubleshooting approach is the difference between repeating the same outage and resolving it efficiently. At its core, systematic troubleshooting means using a consistent sequence of steps to collect facts, form hypotheses, test them, and document outcomes. This prevents 'shotgun troubleshooting' where multiple changes are made at once and nobody knows which change solved the problem. Think of troubleshooting as a scientific method applied to networks: gather observations, propose an explanation, design a test that will confirm or reject the explanation, run the test, and record the result. For example, if a user reports no connectivity and there are no link lights, the likely root cause is physical. If you instead applied high-level fixes, you might waste time reconfiguring services that depend on basic link status. A common misconception is that experience alone replaces process; in reality, without a repeatable method even experienced technicians can overlook simple checks. The practical benefit is measurable: less time spent, fewer repeated outages, and a growing documentation set that accelerates future work. Before you change any configuration, ask: what is my hypothesis and how will this test it?

The OSI model divides network functionality into seven conceptual layers, and that division is an effective diagnostic checklist. When you map observed symptoms to layers, you prioritize checks and avoid irrelevant changes. For instance, a cable failure is a physical layer problem; an incorrect IP address is a network layer issue; and a misconfigured file service is an application layer concern. Using the OSI model means you can rule out whole categories quickly. Start with a claim: where does the symptom best fit — link failure, unreachable IP, or failed login? Then perform the checks associated with that layer. A key benefit is that you can escalate or hand off with precise information: rather than saying 'network is broken,' you can say 'Layer 3 routing to the server is failing,' which focuses subsequent work. A common misconception is to treat the OSI model as rigid order; instead, use it as a guide. Depending on context, you might start at the top or bottom. The important part is isolating the layer so you can apply the right tools and commands. Using the OSI Model as a Diagnostic Framework means map symptoms to layers to focus checks and communicate precise findings to teammates.. In practical terms, a seven-layer checklist for isolating problems. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Layers 1 and 2 are where the network meets physical reality. When a device cannot access any network resources, start here. A basic sequence: visually inspect cable connections, confirm link lights on NIC and switch, check switch port status and VLAN membership, and confirm MAC address presence in the switch table if you have access. These checks are fast and often resolve simple faults caused by loose cables, port moves, or incorrect VLAN assignments. For example, a user whose machine has no link lights likely has a physical issue; re-seating the cable and testing the port typically resolves it. A common misconception is that modern networks 'just work' so we can skip these checks — skipping them wastes time if the root cause is physical. If physical checks pass, move up the layers. Remember to follow safety and access policies before touching equipment. Keep a quick checklist: cable, link lights, port status, VLAN, MAC table. This short routine removes a large portion of transient incidents and gives you confidence to proceed when nothing obvious appears. Physical and Data Link Checks (Layers 1–2) means fast physical and switch-level checks remove many simple causes before deeper investigation.. In practical terms, basic connectivity checks you should always perform first. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Once physical and data link checks are clear, move to Layers 3 and 4. Layer 3 checks address IP addressing and routing: confirm the device has a valid IP, correct subnet mask, and appropriate default gateway. Use ping to verify reachability and tracert to inspect the path a packet takes to a destination. If routing is incorrect, tracert often shows where packets stop being forwarded. At Layer 4, verify transport-level connectivity: ensure the service port is open and the target service is listening. Commands like Test-NetConnection or telnet to a port help determine whether a TCP handshake succeeds. For SMB shares, for example, verify TCP 445. A common misconception is to assume reachability equals service availability; a host can respond to ping but still have its application port blocked by a firewall or not listening. Your hypothesis should reflect the symptom: unreachable IP suggests Layer 3; reachable IP but closed port suggests Layer 4. Always document the commands you ran and their outputs so the next person understands what was tested and why. Network and Transport Layer Checks (Layers 3–4) means use ping and tracert for routing issues; use port checks to confirm services at the transport layer.. In practical terms, ip reachability, routing, and port verification. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Layers 5 through 7 handle sessions, data representation, and the actual application services the user interacts with. When a user can reach an IP and a port but cannot access a service, start looking here. For example, a shared drive that fails to open despite successful port checks could indicate incorrect share paths, permissions, or authentication failures. Verify the user's credentials, check server logs for authentication errors, and confirm the service is configured to accept connections from that client. Presentation issues, like encoding or protocol mismatches, are less common in basic file sharing but can appear in application stacks that require specific negotiation. A helpful approach is to reproduce the failure from another client or from the server itself to distinguish client vs server problems. A frequent misconception is treating application errors as network issues; testing whether the application works locally on the server helps identify where the error originates. Always include these high-level checks before making assumptions about routing or physical causes when service-specific symptoms appear. Session, Presentation, and Application Checks (Layers 5–7) means if reachability and ports are confirmed, investigate sessions, authentication, and application configuration for the root cause.. In practical terms, authentication, sessions, and application configuration issues. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

There are three widely used troubleshooting methodologies and each fits different scenarios. Bottom-up starts at the physical layer and moves upward; it is effective when there is no connectivity at all. Top-down starts at the application layer and moves downward; it is useful when some services are working but a specific application fails. Divide-and-conquer isolates the failing segment or device by comparing affected and unaffected groups, which is powerful when only part of the network is impacted. To choose: when a user has zero network access, bottom-up quickly rules out cabling and ports. When a specific service fails while others work, top-down narrows down service or session issues. If only one department is affected, divide-and-conquer limits focus to that segment. A common error is applying the wrong method and wasting time. For example, running switch port checks (bottom-up) when only one application fails is inefficient. Instead, start where the symptom logically belongs. Each method still benefits from forming a hypothesis and testing it; methodologies guide your starting point and order of checks, not replace disciplined testing and documentation. Let's walk a real scenario: a user cannot access \\fileserver\shared but can browse the internet. Step one, define the problem precisely: confirm the exact path, the error message, and whether other users have the same issue. Step two, gather information: ping the file server IP, run tracert, and test TCP 445 with Test-NetConnection or telnet. If ping succeeds and port 445 is reachable, move to higher-layer checks: verify credentials and server share permissions and look for authentication failures in logs. If the port is closed or tracert fails, the fault is likely Layer 3 or 4 and you should investigate routing and firewall rules. Use divide-and-conquer if only one department is affected — test from a different segment. Form a hypothesis, for example, 'SMB port blocked by a firewall rule between the user and server,' and design a test like temporarily allowing the port for the client segment. Make one change at a time. After confirmation, implement the permanent fix and document the exact commands, the successful test results, and preventative recommendations.
